title: Lumbar WBCT vs MRI
official: Standing Weight-Bearing Cone-Beam CT and Clinical Phenotype Concordance in Lumbar Degenerative Radiculopathy
summary:
Patients with pain in their low back that sometimes sends a shooting, sharp pain down their leg are usually diagnosed with lumbar radicular pain, or lumbar radiculopathy. MRIs are most commonly used to acquire images of the spine. The purpose of these images is to provide doctors with important information on what may be causing the low back pain and what treatment options may be the most effective in treating the pain. However, standard MRIs are taken when the patient is lying down, which may not be the most accurate representation of what the spine looks like in positions where patients experience pain, such as standing. A weight-bearing CT (WBCT) scan is a 3D imaging test that takes detailed pictures of the spine while patients are standing up. Unlike traditional MRI scans, where the patient lies down, this technology provides more information on how the spine looks when the patient is upright and participating in activities such as standing and walking. This information allows doctors to better understand the underlying causes of the pain and help guide targeted treatments to address those issues.

The Planmed XFI full-body weight-bearing CT scanner received 510(k) clearance from the FDA on September 26, 2025. This means the Planmed XFI® WBCT is safe and effective because it is substantially equivalent to a device already on the market.
criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:

* Age ≥45 years.
* Predominant unilateral lumbar radicular pain and/or paresthesias. True bilateral radicular presentations are excluded.
* Lumbar radicular pattern on chart-review screening - a coarse eligibility filter only. Root level is not assigned at screening; it is assigned by the blinded standardized examination after enrollment (§8).
* Ability to stand unsupported to undergo study examination and WBCT.
* Informed consent, including broad re-contact consent and consent to outcomes follow-up.

Exclusion Criteria:

A candidate meeting any of the following is excluded:

1. True bilateral or symmetric radicular presentation with no dominant symptomatic side. The side-contrast endpoint (§10.3) requires an asymptomatic homolog. Unilaterally dominant presentations with minor contralateral involvement are eligible; isolated laterality is recorded and drives a clean-unilateral sensitivity analysis.
2. Radicular symptoms attributable to a non-degenerative cause - neoplasm, infection, inflammatory or autoimmune disease, acute fracture, or other non-degenerative structural lesion at the symptomatic level.
3. Any prior lumbar spine surgery - instrumented fusion, posterior instrumentation, decompression, or discectomy. Altered biomechanics, junctional change, and retained/residual disc or epidural fibrosis distort foraminal and segmental anatomy and confound both measurement and symptom attribution.
4. Any lumbar spine procedure in the last 12 weeks - including any epidural steroid injection, radiofrequency nerve ablation, facet injection, medial branch block or SI joint injection
5. Inability to stand and hold the neutral and extension positions for acquisition with no more than light bilateral fingertip contact - from a balance disorder, orthostatic intolerance, lower-limb weakness, weight-bearing restriction, or pain that precludes positioning.
6. Pregnancy or possibility of pregnancy. Screening and testing per institutional and RSO policy (§13).
7. BMI \> 35 kg/m2. Cone-beam image quality degrades with soft-tissue path length independently of dose, and osseous depiction becomes diagnostically unusable in the 32-35 range (Benz 2018). Because the primary endpoint is a bony-boundary geometric measurement, quality loss translates directly into measurement error. Set pre-emptively rather than by post-acquisition exclusion, which would irradiate participants whose acquisitions are predictably unusable.
8. Inability to provide informed consent, or insufficient capacity to understand and communicate symptoms for the standardized phenotype examination (§8).
